items.title: A complete-or-weakly-sparse blockade can be thinned to equal subblocks with directional sparsity
items.strategy: Choose equal-size subsets inside the blocks one at a time, deleting vertices that are too heavy against already fixed subblocks and against the untouched future blocks. The weak edge-density bounds make each deletion small enough that the surviving subsets keep the prescribed common size, and every formerly weakly sparse pair becomes directionally sparse in both directions after the loss bookkeeping.

items.title: A complete-or-weakly-sparse blockade yields a complete subblockade or an anticonnected thinning
items.strategy: First thin the blockade by the previous lemma so that noncomplete pairs are directionally sparse at a slightly weaker exponent. If some thinned block has only small anticonnected components, the published anticonnected-component lemma gives a complete blockade of the target length and width. Otherwise choose one large anticonnected component from each thinned block and trim them to a common size; completeness is inherited and the directional sparse bounds survive the trimming.

items.title: A wonderful anticonnected complete-or-sparse blockade yields a restricted subgraph or a large anticomplete pair
items.strategy: Apply wonderfulness to the anticonnected equal-size blockade. If it returns the restricted induced subgraph, keep that outcome. Otherwise fix a block with few mixed outside vertices, use y-sparsity to bound outside vertices that still have many neighbors into that block, subtract the total mass of the blockade itself, and conclude that almost all remaining outside vertices are anticomplete to the chosen block.

items.title: Generalized niceness yields four reduction outcomes
items.strategy: Handle the small-graph case first. If the complement is y-sparse, apply the published leaf-reducible lemma in the complement and translate its complete pair or restricted-set outcome back to G. Otherwise G is y-sparse, so apply generalized niceness at epsilon = y^a, where a is the wonderfulness exponent. Three of the four generalized-nice outcomes already match the target list after exponent renaming; in the remaining blockade case, pass through the anticonnected thinning lemma and then the wonderfulness lemma.

items.title: Large almost-pure pair hypotheses yield a complete or anticomplete blockade
items.strategy: Repeat the maximal-blockade proof used for the published sparse-or-complete extraction theorem, but replace the sparse relation by anticomplete throughout. The last block can always be split by the hypothesis unless the blockade is already long enough, and once the maximal blockade has length at least twice the target one of the two relation types occupies at least half the blocks.

items.title: cy-restricted generalized niceness yields three outcomes
items.strategy: Fix the cutoff c from the previous four-outcome lemma. If every c|G|-large induced subgraph already has a large complete or anticomplete pair, the new corollary gives the blockade outcome directly. Otherwise choose a large induced subgraph where that pair fails. Restrictedness passes to induced subgraphs, so applying the four-outcome lemma there leaves only the clique-or-stable-set outcome, the smaller-scale restricted-set outcome, or a blockade that is still large enough in the original graph.

items.title: Iterated restricted sparsification reaches the target scale
items.strategy: Follow the minimal-parameter iterative-sparsification proof from the lecture notes: among all restricted induced subgraphs large enough for their current scale, choose one whose scale parameter is minimal. The second hypothesis would then force a strictly smaller admissible scale unless the chosen subgraph is already x-restricted, and the product inequality turns the resulting size bound into the required x-scale lower bound.

items.title: A large cy-restricted subgraph in the three-outcome theorem forces a smaller-scale restricted subgraph
items.strategy: Apply the three-outcome theorem to the large cy-restricted subgraph F. If that theorem yields a clique or stable set, or a complete or anticomplete blockade, the assumed failure of the global outcomes is contradicted by direct exponent comparisons between |F| and |G|. Therefore only the smaller-scale restricted induced subgraph can survive, which is exactly the claim needed for the final iterative step.

items.title: Constant-scale restricted generalized niceness yields an x-scale restricted subgraph, a polynomial clique or stable set, or a blockade
items.strategy: Assume the clique-or-stable-set and blockade outcomes fail. The previous claim then verifies the second hypothesis of the restricted iterative-sparsification lemma with the source choice b1 = c4/2, b2 = 4c3/c4, and b3 = c3, while the three-outcome theorem supplies the starting c-restricted subgraph. Because c4 >= 4, the inequality b1 b2 >= b2 + b3 holds, so the iterative lemma returns the required x-scale restricted induced subgraph.

title: Generalized Niceness and Reduction Outcomes -- Examples

items.title: Thinning a four-block weakly sparse blockade to directional sparse subblocks
items.strategy: Take four equal blocks with a single cross-edge witnessing each noncomplete pair, remove the vertices incident with those edges, and check the remaining equal-size subblocks directly. The calculation shows on a finite model how a weak edge-density bound becomes directional sparsity after the thinning step.

items.title: A large almost-pure pair extends an anticomplete blockade
items.strategy: Start from a last block B_n together with explicit anticomplete subsets X and Y inside it that satisfy the size bounds of the corollary. Replacing B_n by X and Y shows concretely how the maximality contradiction grows an anticomplete blockade by one step.

items.title: A numeric run of the Lemma 3.3 exponent choice
items.strategy: Choose sample source constants with c4 = 4 and c3 > 0, compute b1 = c4/2, b2 = 4c3/c4, and b3 = c3, verify the product inequality exactly, and then run the size comparisons in the helper claim and the final lemma for concrete x, c, and y.
